feedback: If the pupil just repeats the action ('they recycle'), ask 'what does recycling actually do to the materials, and why is that better than landfill?' to force the mechanism.
If the pupil says solar is good because it's 'clean and green', ask 'where does the electricity come from if there are NO panels?' to supply the fossil-fuel comparison.
If the pupil gives a cost reason ('the electricity is free'), acknowledge the saving, then ask specifically what happens to the air or pollution when less fossil fuel is burned.

If the pupil thinks a cloudy week makes the panels useless, ask whether they still help overall across a year: panels produce less in cloudy weather but still generate some electricity, and over a year their total output can replace electricity that would otherwise come from burning fossil fuels.
If the pupil dismisses effort as pointless ('one town is too small to matter'), build from one to many: revisit how individual solutions add up when a whole community combines them.
Reinforce when the pupil both traces a full causal chain AND notes how many efforts combine.
activities.intendedInsight: Protecting resources means pairing a science mechanism (e.g. sunlight → electricity → less fossil fuel burned) with collective action; the science idea is only half the story, and the power comes from many people combining the same action.
learnerActions: Take on the role of a reporter and interview a community-project lead in role — e.g. a solar-co-op organiser, a reforestation ranger, a recycling-scheme coordinator.
Ask the blunt, evidence-seeking question: 'Does putting panels on roofs really make a difference? How does it actually help?'

Record the mechanism the character gives, e.g. 'sunlight becomes electricity, so power stations need to burn less fossil fuel such as coal or gas (where the local electricity comes from them), so less CO₂ goes up — here's how many homes we've switched.'
Respond to the character's flip-question — 'one roof is tiny, so why do we sign up whole streets at once?' — and explain in your own words why many people combining the same small action matters.
Interview at least two more leads (reforestation ranger, recycling coordinator) and note the same shape of argument: a science mechanism paired with collective action.
After the interviews, compare how well each solution works and where it might have costs or trade-offs.
activities.title: Interview the people doing the protecting

feedback: For a wrong match, restate the action and ask 'what does this physically do, and why does that help the environment?'

If the pupil miscategorises an energy source, revisit what 'renewable' means: a source that is naturally replenished on human timescales (like sunlight or wind), versus fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) that took millions of years to form and are used up much faster than they can be replaced. Burning fossil fuels also releases CO₂, but burning is not what makes a source non-renewable.
If the pupil tries to force recycling, composting or reforestation into the renewable-vs-fossil sort, clarify these are resource-protection actions, not ways of generating electricity.
activities.intendedInsight: Each protective action is backed by a specific science mechanism, and many people's actions combining at community scale multiply the effect; among energy sources, renewables are naturally replenished while fossil fuels take millions of years to form and run out, and burning them also releases CO₂.
learnerActions: Match each action (solar panels, recycling, reforestation, wind turbine, composting) to the science idea that explains why it helps.
Answer a question on why combining many people's actions at community scale produces a measurable effect that a single household's action alone cannot.

Sort only the energy-generation examples into renewable (e.g. solar, wind) versus non-renewable/fossil-fuel (e.g. coal, gas, oil); note that recycling, composting and reforestation protect resources in other ways and are not energy sources, so they do not belong in either energy category.
activities.title: Match the action to its science idea
